evals.prompt: We're adding team workspaces to our SaaS: users can invite others by email, share projects across a workspace, and admins can export all workspace data as CSV. Design doc is in docs/rfcs/workspaces.md. Before we build it, what could go wrong security-wise?
evals.expected_output: A threat model grounded in the design doc: data-flow edges, trust boundaries (tenant to shared service, invite links, export), assets, attacker profiles, STRIDE-derived abuse paths ranked by likelihood x impact, specific mitigations with owners, and explicit residual risk.
expectations: Reads docs/rfcs/workspaces.md and lists components and data flows from it, labelling assumptions
Identifies cross-workspace (tenant) data access as a high-priority abuse path with a specific per-object authorization mitigation
Covers invite-link threats such as token guessing, replay, or invite to an attacker-controlled email
Treats the CSV export as a boundary (data leaving access control, or CSV/formula injection)
Each threat has likelihood and impact ratings with justifications, and mitigations name a location and an owner
Includes a residual-risk section or states that none remains

evals.prompt: Our support bot is getting new tools: it can look up a customer's orders, issue refunds up to $50, and read our help-center articles plus the customer's previous emails. Can you threat model this quickly? Leadership wants to ship Friday.
evals.expected_output: Despite time pressure, the model treats emails and articles as attacker-controlled content, identifies indirect prompt injection leading to unauthorized refunds or cross-customer data exposure, and proposes controls outside the model (scoped credentials, per-customer enforcement, refund caps and confirmations).
expectations: Identifies indirect prompt injection via customer emails or help-center content as a threat
Identifies the refund tool as the highest-impact tool, with abuse via injection or social engineering
Mitigations are enforced outside the model (e.g. customer scoping in the tool, per-conversation refund limits, human approval), not only prompt wording
Addresses cross-customer data leakage through the order lookup tool
Still produces a ranked list with named residual risks rather than skipping ranking because of the deadline

evals.prompt: Do a STRIDE analysis of our webhook receiver in services/billing/webhooks/ — it takes Stripe events and updates subscription status.
evals.expected_output: An evidence-based model of the existing receiver: checks whether signatures and timestamps are verified in code, covers replay, spoofing, out-of-order events, and DoS, and distinguishes existing controls (with file:line) from recommended ones.
expectations: Cites file:line evidence for whether webhook signature verification exists
Covers replay or timestamp tolerance, and idempotency of event handling
Addresses tampering or ordering of subscription state (e.g. out-of-order events)
Distinguishes existing mitigations from recommended ones
Does not present generic threats with no asset or impact
